habitat: Open country with bushes, farming areas, and arid shrublands; often seen near water bodies.
diet: Predominantly insectivorous, specializing in bees, wasps, and ants caught in mid-air flight.
distribution: Widespread across South and Southeast Asia, from Iran to Vietnam.
ecologicalRole: Insect predator that helps maintain the balance of flying insect populations.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Before eating a bee or wasp, it removes the stinger by repeatedly thrashing the insect against its perch.

habitat: Open or well-wooded areas, gardens, urban parks, and groves with fruiting trees.
diet: Mainly frugivorous, feeding on figs and berries; also takes nectar and occasional insects.
distribution: Found across the Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka.
ecologicalRole: Seed disperser, especially for Ficus species in urban and forest ecosystems.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Known for its distinctive, repetitive 'kutroo-kutroo-kutroo' call that can be heard throughout the day.

habitat: Grasslands, pastures, and agricultural fields; frequently follows grazing cattle or tractors.
diet: Insects such as grasshoppers and flies; also feeds on frogs, lizards, and small mammals.
distribution: Cosmopolitan; found globally across most continents.
ecologicalRole: Forages alongside livestock, consuming insects stirred up by their movement.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Unlike other egrets, it is much less dependent on water and is often found in dry terrestrial habitats.

habitat: Still or slow-flowing fresh water, including rivers, canals, lakes, and ponds with vegetated banks.
diet: Primarily small fish; also consumes aquatic insects, crustaceans, and tadpoles.
distribution: Widespread across Eurasia, North Africa, and parts of the Indian subcontinent.
ecologicalRole: Freshwater predator and bioindicator of aquatic health.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: It can dive into water at high speeds, using a nictitating membrane to protect its eyes underwater.

habitat: Open woodlands, agricultural lands, and highly urbanized environments.
diet: Omnivorous; feeds on insects, fruits, seeds, and human food scraps.
distribution: Native to Asia; widely introduced to many other parts of the world.
ecologicalRole: Insect controller that has adapted successfully to urban environments.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Often called the 'farmer's friend' in India because it consumes large quantities of crop-destroying grasshoppers.

habitat: Scrubland, forest edges, thickets near water, and mountain meadows.
diet: Mainly seeds, buds, and berries; occasionally takes insects during the breeding season.
distribution: Widespread across Northern Eurasia; winters in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
ecologicalRole: Seed predator and disperser.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Moderate Conservation Priority; Current Trend: Rapid Decline. Protected under Schedule II of Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Males take two years to acquire their bright red 'rose' plumage; younger males look similar to the brown females.

habitat: Open forests, gardens, scrubland, and urban parks with dense shrubbery.
diet: Primarily small insects, larvae, and spiders; also visits flowers for nectar.
distribution: Found across tropical South Asia and Southeast Asia.
ecologicalRole: Insectivore that helps control pest populations in gardens.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Increasing. Protected under Schedule II of Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Constructs its nest by sewing leaves together using spider silk or plant fibers, using its sharp bill as a needle.

habitat: Gardens, groves, urban areas, and sparse woodland with old trees.
diet: Mainly frugivorous, preferring wild figs and berries; occasionally eats insects.
distribution: Widespread across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
ecologicalRole: Seed disperser in both urban and rural ecosystems.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Its name comes from its repetitive call that sounds like a coppersmith striking metal with a hammer.

habitat: Forest and plantation; shady forest floor, woodland clearings, and wooded gardens with leaf litter.
diet: Mainly insects and other small invertebrates found by foraging on the ground.
distribution: Breeds in Northeast Asia; winters in South India, Southeast Asia, and Indonesia.
ecologicalRole: Ground-dwelling insectivore of forested habitats.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: High Conservation Priority; Trend: Rapid Decline. Protected under Schedule I of Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Unlike other wagtails, it swings its tail from side to side rather than up and down.

habitat: Fast-flowing mountain streams for breeding; varied wetlands and canal edges in winter.
diet: Aquatic and terrestrial insects, especially flies and larvae.
distribution: Widespread across Eurasia and Africa; winters in South Asia.
ecologicalRole: Insectivore near water bodies.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Moderate Conservation Priority; Current Trend: Rapid Decline. Protected under Schedule II of Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Possesses a much longer tail than other wagtails, which it wags constantly while standing.

habitat: Open landscapes with short vegetation, orchards, vineyards, and parkland.
diet: Ground-dwelling insects and their larvae, spiders, and occasionally small reptiles.
distribution: Found across Europe, Asia, and North Africa.
ecologicalRole: Controller of ground-dwelling insect pests.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Moderate Conservation Priority; Trend: Decline. Protected under Schedule II of Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: It uses its long, decurved bill to probe deep into the soil to find grubs and mole crickets.

habitat: Urban and suburban areas; strictly associated with human settlements.
diet: Omnivorous scavenger; eats everything from insects and small animals to human waste.
distribution: Native to South Asia; widely introduced as an invasive species in Africa and Europe.
ecologicalRole: Scavenger in urban ecosystems, helping to dispose of waste.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: It is closely associated with human habitation and is rarely found living away from cities, towns, or villages.

habitat: Open woodland, urban parks, and groves with large fruiting trees like Banyan and Peepal.
diet: Primarily frugivorous, especially figs; also takes insects, small reptiles, and bird nestlings.
distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent.
ecologicalRole: Seed disperser for many tropical tree species due to its wide ranging flight.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: The female seals herself inside a tree hollow during nesting, relying entirely on the male to feed her through a narrow slit.

habitat: Deciduous forests, scrubland, and agricultural fields; often found near human habitation.
diet: Omnivorous; feeds on seeds, fruits, insects, small reptiles, and amphibians.
distribution: Native to South Asia; introduced to many countries worldwide.
ecologicalRole: Generalist feeder; helps control small snakes and insect populations.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Increasing. Protected under Schedule I of Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: The National Bird of India. The 'eyes' on its train are used in a vibrating display to attract females.

habitat: Scrub jungle, deciduous forests, and dense undergrowth with moist leaf litter.
diet: Insects, earthworms, and snails found by foraging on the forest floor.
distribution: Breeds in the Himalayas and Central India; winters in Southern India and Sri Lanka.
ecologicalRole: Forest floor insectivore.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Known as 'Navrang' (Nine Colors) in many Indian languages due to its brilliant multi-colored plumage.

habitat: Open grasslands, cultivated fields, and light forests; often seen on roadside power lines.
diet: Mainly insects like beetles and crickets; also takes lizards, frogs, and small snakes.
distribution: Found across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
ecologicalRole: Biological pest controller in agricultural landscapes.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Named for its spectacular aerial acrobatics ('rolling') during the breeding season.

habitat: Open woodland, scrubland, and well-vegetated gardens.
diet: Mainly insects; also eats berries, grains, and nectar.
distribution: Endemic to the Indian subcontinent.
ecologicalRole: Social bird that helps maintain ecosystem balance through insectivory.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Commonly known as 'Seven Sisters' because they are almost always found in small, noisy groups.

habitat: Wet meadows, marshes, and agricultural fields near water bodies.
diet: Insects, earthworms, and other small invertebrates.
distribution: Widespread across Eurasia; winters in Northern India.
ecologicalRole: Ground-foraging insectivore.
conservationStatus: Near Threatened (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Moderate Conservation Priority; Trend: Decline. Protected under Schedule II of Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Known for its distinctive 'peewit' call and unique crest, which it can raise when excited.

habitat: Open fields, marshes, and margins of water bodies; often found near human habitation.
diet: Insects, snails, and other invertebrates; occasionally feeds on grains.
distribution: Found from West Asia through the Indian subcontinent to Southeast Asia.
ecologicalRole: Ground-nesting insectivore that acts as a sentinel for other species.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Its alarm call is famously interpreted as 'Did-he-do-it?', often used to alert other animals to danger.

habitat: Large rivers, lakes, and salt marshes; often found in open areas near water.
diet: Omnivorous; feeds on grasses, seeds, aquatic plants, insects, and small fish.
distribution: Breeds in Central Asia and SE Europe; winters throughout the Indian subcontinent.
ecologicalRole: Grazing waterfowl that impacts both aquatic and terrestrial vegetation.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: Known in India as the 'Brahminy Duck', it is often seen in pairs and is known for its loud, honking calls.

habitat: Open woodland, deciduous forests, gardens, and groves.
diet: Highly omnivorous; eats fruits, seeds, insects, lizards, and small birds.
distribution: Found throughout South Asia and Southeast Asia.
ecologicalRole: Generalist predator and scavenger that also aids in seed dispersal.
conservationStatus: Least Concern (IUCN). SoIB 2023: Low Conservation Priority; Trend: Stable. Not protected under Wildlife (Protection) Act.
interestingFact: A member of the crow family, it has a wide repertoire of calls, including musical notes and harsh rattles.

habitat: Open wetlands, marshes, and flooded agricultural fields, particularly rice paddies.
diet: Omnivorous; consumes aquatic plants, seeds, insects, crustaceans, and small vertebrates.

ecologicalRole: Indicator of healthy wetland ecosystems.

habitat: Diverse habitats including gardens, forests, agricultural fields, and near water bodies.

habitat: Marshes, ponds, canals, and ditches with thick emergent vegetation.
